q: WAPDA (Water and Power Development Authority) was established in:
explanation: WAPDA was created under the Pakistan Water and Power Development Authority Act, 1958, to develop water and power resources in a unified way.
why: Year of the war with India.

q: WAPDA headquarters (WAPDA House) is located in:
explanation: WAPDA House is a landmark on The Mall, Lahore.
why: Federal capital, but not WAPDA HQ.

q: After the restructuring of the power sector (WAPDA bifurcation, 2007), WAPDA’s core responsibility is:
options: Development of water resources and hydropower
explanation: Distribution moved to DISCOs, transmission to NTDC and tariff regulation to NEPRA; WAPDA retained water and hydropower development and operation.
why: Thermal GENCOs were separated from WAPDA.

q: Tarbela Dam is built on the river:
explanation: Tarbela on the Indus (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) is one of the largest earth- and rock-filled dams in the world and Pakistan’s largest hydropower station.
why: No major WAPDA storage dam on the Chenab.
Warsak is on the Kabul River.

q: Mangla Dam is located on the river:
explanation: Mangla Dam (Mirpur, AJK) on the Jhelum was completed in 1967 under the Indus Basin Project.
why: Mohmand Dam is on the Swat River.
Ravi is an eastern river allocated to India.

q: Pakistan’s largest hydropower station by installed capacity is:
explanation: Tarbela’s installed capacity is 4,888 MW after the 4th extension (1,410 MW), and it rises to 6,418 MW with the 5th extension (1,530 MW).

q: The Tarbela 4th Extension Hydropower Project added an installed capacity of:
explanation: T4 has 3 units of 470 MW = 1,410 MW, built on tunnel 4. T5 (3 × 510 MW = 1,530 MW) is on tunnel 5.

q: Ghazi Barotha Hydropower Project, a run-of-river plant on the Indus, has an installed capacity of:
explanation: Five units of 290 MW = 1,450 MW. Water is diverted at Ghazi barrage through a ~52 km power channel to the powerhouse at Barotha.

q: Warsak Dam and hydropower station is on the:
explanation: Warsak (near Peshawar) on the Kabul River was completed around 1960; installed capacity about 243 MW.
why: Kunhar hosts smaller projects (e.g. Suki Kinari, Patrind on its confluence).
Mohmand Dam is on the Swat River.

q: Neelum–Jhelum Hydropower Project has an installed capacity of:
explanation: Four units of 242.25 MW = 969 MW; Neelum water is diverted through a long headrace tunnel to a powerhouse near Muzaffarabad. Completed in 2018.

q: Dasu Hydropower Project is located on the:
explanation: Dasu (Upper Kohistan, KP) is a run-of-river project on the Indus with planned capacity of 4,320 MW (Stage-I 2,160 MW).
why: Mangla and Karot are on the Jhelum.

q: Planned installed capacity of Diamer-Bhasha Dam is about:
explanation: Diamer-Bhasha on the Indus is planned for about 4,500 MW, with a roller-compacted concrete (RCC) dam about 272 m high.

q: Mohmand Dam is being built on the:
explanation: Mohmand Dam (Mohmand district, KP) on the Swat River: concrete-faced rockfill dam with about 800 MW hydropower, plus flood control, irrigation and water supply to Peshawar.
why: Warsak is on the Kabul River.
Kurram Tangi is on the Kurram.

q: Which of the following is a run-of-river project rather than a large storage reservoir?
explanation: Ghazi Barotha uses the flow released from Tarbela via a pondage and power channel; it has no large seasonal storage.

q: The Indus Waters Treaty between Pakistan and India was signed in:
explanation: Signed in Karachi in September 1960 with the World Bank as broker (and signatory for certain provisions).
why: Year of the inter-dominion water dispute/standstill.

q: Under the Indus Waters Treaty, the western rivers allocated to Pakistan are:
explanation: Western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan; eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India.
why: Sutlej is eastern; the Kabul is not covered as a treaty river.

q: Which institution brokered the Indus Waters Treaty?
explanation: The World Bank (then IBRD) brokered the treaty and helped finance the Indus Basin Project (Mangla, Tarbela, link canals).

q: NEPRA was established under an Act passed in:
explanation: National Electric Power Regulatory Authority — Regulation of Generation, Transmission and Distribution of Electric Power Act, 1997.

q: The main function of NEPRA is to:
options: Regulate the power sector: licences, tariffs and performance standards
explanation: NEPRA grants licences for generation, transmission and distribution, determines tariffs and enforces performance standards.

q: In Pakistan, the 500 kV and 220 kV transmission network is operated by:
explanation: NTDC owns and operates the primary 500/220 kV grid and grid stations, and national dispatch has historically been with its National Power Control Centre. DISCOs operate 132 kV and below.

q: The voltage level normally used for primary distribution feeders by DISCOs in Pakistan is:
explanation: 11 kV feeders from grid stations supply distribution transformers (11 kV/400 V). 132 kV and 66 kV are sub-transmission; 500/220 kV are transmission.
why: That is LV supply to consumers.

q: Standard system frequency in Pakistan is:
explanation: Pakistan uses 50 Hz (like most of Asia and Europe). 60 Hz is used in North America and parts of other regions.
why: Used in the USA and Saudi Arabia.

q: Low-voltage supply to consumers in Pakistan is nominally:
explanation: Single-phase 230 V (often quoted as 220 V) and three-phase 400 V line-to-line (from 11 kV/0.4 kV transformers).
why: That is the North American style.

q: Pakistan’s first HVDC transmission line (CPEC) connects:
explanation: The ±660 kV, 4,000 MW Matiari (Sindh) to Lahore HVDC line (about 880 km) was commissioned in 2021 to carry power from southern coal plants to the north.

q: The operating voltage of the Matiari–Lahore HVDC line is:
explanation: It is a ±660 kV bipole rated 4,000 MW.
why: An AC level, not this line.

q: K-Electric supplies electricity mainly to:
explanation: K-Electric (formerly KESC, privatised in 2005) is a vertically integrated utility serving Karachi and adjoining areas.

q: LESCO, GEPCO, FESCO, IESCO and MEPCO are examples of:
explanation: DISCOs distribute electricity in their regions: Lahore, Gujranwala, Faisalabad, Islamabad, Multan (and PESCO, HESCO, SEPCO, QESCO, TESCO).

q: The company serving Multan region as a DISCO is:
explanation: MEPCO = Multan Electric Power Company.

q: The Private Power and Infrastructure Board (PPIB) mainly:
explanation: PPIB acts as a one-window facilitator for independent power producers.

q: Chashma and K-2/K-3 are examples of Pakistan’s:
explanation: Chashma (C-1 to C-4) in Punjab and K-2/K-3 (Hualong One units of about 1,100 MW each) near Karachi are operated by the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC). Chashma also has a separate low-head hydropower station.
why: Wind farms are in the Jhimpir–Gharo corridor.
Chashma does have a hydel plant, but C-1…C-4 and K-2/K-3 are nuclear.
Coal plants include Sahiwal, Port Qasim, Hub and Thar.

q: Thar coalfield, used for mine-mouth power generation, is located in:
explanation: Thar (Tharparkar district, Sindh) holds very large lignite reserves; several mine-mouth plants operate there.
why: Balochistan has smaller coal fields (e.g. Duki).
Punjab has the Salt Range coal.

q: The Jhimpir–Gharo wind corridor is located in:
explanation: Wind farms in Thatta district, Sindh, benefit from strong coastal winds.

q: The Quaid-e-Azam Solar Park is located near:
explanation: It is in the Cholistan desert near Bahawalpur, Punjab.

q: The Indus River originates in:
explanation: The Indus rises in Tibet near Mount Kailash/Lake Mansarovar and flows through Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan into Pakistan.
why: The Jhelum rises in the Kashmir valley (Verinag).

q: The Water Apportionment Accord distributing Indus waters among the provinces was signed in:
explanation: The 1991 Accord apportioned water among Punjab, Sindh, KP and Balochistan; IRSA was set up in 1992 to implement it.

q: Water distribution among the provinces according to the 1991 Accord is regulated by:
explanation: IRSA, established by an Act of 1992, regulates and monitors distribution of Indus waters among provinces.

q: Rawal Dam, supplying water to Rawalpindi/Islamabad, is on the:
explanation: Rawal Dam: Kurang River. Simly Dam: Soan River. Khanpur Dam: Haro River.

q: Mirani Dam in Balochistan is on the:
explanation: Mirani Dam (Kech district, near Turbat) on the Dasht River supplies irrigation water. Hub Dam is on the Hub River.

q: Tarbela and Mangla are called multipurpose projects because they provide:
options: Irrigation storage, hydropower and flood mitigation
explanation: Their primary purpose is storage for irrigation; hydropower and flood moderation are additional benefits.
why: Power is one of several purposes.
Drinking water is a minor use.

q: Most large hydropower units in Pakistan (e.g. at Tarbela and Mangla) use:
explanation: Medium-head storage dams typically use Francis (reaction) turbines; Pelton suits very high heads and Kaplan low heads.
why: For low heads (e.g. some barrage/canal plants).

q: A major operational problem for Pakistan’s reservoirs such as Tarbela is:
explanation: The Indus carries a heavy silt load; sedimentation steadily reduces live storage and threatens intakes, which is why new storage (Bhasha, Mohmand) is prioritised.
why: Not a concern at these dams.

q: The Ministry under which WAPDA currently functions is the:
explanation: Since the creation of the Ministry of Water Resources (2018), WAPDA functions under it; DISCOs and NTDC are under the Power Division.

q: Satpara Dam, providing water and power to Skardu, is in:
explanation: Satpara Dam lies near Skardu, Gilgit-Baltistan.

q: Gomal Zam Dam is located in:
explanation: Gomal Zam on the Gomal River (South Waziristan) provides irrigation and a small hydropower station.

q: Why is reactive power support (capacitor banks/SVCs) important on long 11 kV rural feeders in Pakistan?
options: To reduce the number of consumers
To reduce voltage drop and line losses caused by low power factor loads
explanation: Low-pf loads (motors, tube-wells) draw extra current; shunt compensation reduces current, voltage drop and I^{2}R losses on long feeders.
why: Capacitors do not store energy for hours.
Frequency is set by generation–load balance on the grid.

q: Which DISCO serves the Hyderabad region of Sindh?
explanation: HESCO = Hyderabad Electric Supply Company; SEPCO = Sukkur; QESCO = Quetta; PESCO = Peshawar.

q: Karot Hydropower Project (720 MW), developed under CPEC, is on the:
explanation: Karot is a run-of-river plant on the Jhelum near Rawalpindi/AJK border.

q: Suki Kinari Hydropower Project (884 MW) is on the:
explanation: Suki Kinari, in Kaghan valley (Mansehra), is on the Kunhar River.

q: The Tarbela 5th Extension Hydropower Project has a planned installed capacity of:
explanation: T5: 3 × 510 MW = 1,530 MW, taking Tarbela to 6,418 MW.

q: K-Electric (formerly KESC) was privatised in:
explanation: KESC was privatised in 2005 and later renamed K-Electric.

q: The highest AC transmission voltage widely used in Pakistan’s national grid (as of 2026) is:
explanation: 500 kV is the backbone; 765 kV has been planned for evacuating power from Dasu.

q: In the Neelum–Jhelum project, water from the Neelum River is diverted through a tunnel to a powerhouse near:
explanation: Diversion at Nauseri, headrace tunnel to the underground powerhouse at Chattar Klas near Muzaffarabad; tailrace into the Jhelum.
